introduction-moving-beyond-the-basics.core: Bash's power is in combining small single-purpose tools into an automated production line. Mastery means doing that safely and predictably.

first_principles.problem: Knowing individual commands isn't enough. Untrusted scripts fail silently, leave messes behind and break on odd inputs.
truths: Unix tools each do one job well.
Bash wires them together.
Bash's defaults are permissive and unsafe.
derivation: Add **strict mode and traps** for safety.
Use **expansions and arrays** instead of external tools.

analogy.title: A workshop production line
analogy.story: Each hand tool does one job; the production line chains them so they build something complex automatically.
analogy.breaks: Past a few hundred lines, or once real data structures are involved, a real programming language is better.

example.title: A backup script
example.scenario: It grows from 3 lines to a robust tool over this topic.

steps.label: Goal
steps.detail: A script you can trust to run unattended.

check.a: Wiring small single-purpose Unix tools together into automated pipelines.

the-power-of-the-pipe.core: A pipe connects one program's stdout to the next program's stdin, so data streams through small tools with no temporary files.

first_principles.problem: Without pipes you would write intermediate files between every step, which is slow, cluttered and wasteful.
truths: Programs read stdin and write stdout.
Small tools are reusable.
Streaming avoids storing intermediate results.
derivation: Data **flows through** with no temp files.

analogy.title: A factory assembly line
analogy.story: Stamp, drill, paint: each station hands the part straight to the next and nothing piles up in between.
analogy.breaks: Only stdout goes through the pipe. stderr bypasses it unless you redirect it.

example.title: Top 5 IPs in an access log

code.text: cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5

check.q: Does a pipe carry error messages?
check.a: No, only stdout. stderr goes straight to the terminal unless redirected.

redirection-basics-and-2.core: Every process has three streams: stdin (0), stdout (1) and stderr (2). Redirection sends them to files: `>` overwrites, `>>` appends and `2>` captures errors.

first_principles.problem: Output and errors mix on the terminal, and logs are lost when the session closes.
truths: File descriptors 0, 1 and 2 exist for every process.
By default they all point at the terminal.
Separate streams let you treat errors differently.

analogy.title: Three pipes coming out of a machine
analogy.story: Product, waste and intake each have their own pipe, and you can route each one to a different bucket.
analogy.breaks: `>` truncates without asking, so one typo can wipe a file.

example.title: Separating results from errors
example.scenario: Keep good output and errors in different files.

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: found.txt is clean and the permission-denied noise is in errors.txt.

example.outcome: streams go exactly where you want.

check.a: > overwrites the file; >> appends to it.

advanced-redirection-21-and-here-docs.core: `2>&1` points stderr at wherever stdout currently goes, so both end up in one log. Here-docs feed multi-line text into a command's stdin inline.

first_principles.problem: Cron jobs lose their errors because only stdout is logged, and embedding multi-line config with many echo calls is messy.
truths: Redirections are processed left to right.
`2>&1` copies fd 1's current target.
Commands accept input on stdin.
derivation: `2>&1 > log` sends errors to the terminal, which is wrong.

analogy.title: Merging two hoses into one bucket
analogy.story: First aim the main hose at the bucket, then clip the second hose onto the first.
analogy.breaks: If you clip the second hose on first and then move the main one, the second still points at the old place.

example.title: Cron job logging plus a generated config

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Every error lands in the log, and the config is written in one block.

example.outcome: complete logs and clean inline input.

points: Quote EOF to keep the text literal.

check.q: Why does `2>&1 > log` not log errors?
check.a: 2>&1 copies stdout's target (the terminal) before stdout is moved to the log.

exit-codes-did-it-work.core: Every command leaves an integer exit status: 0 means success and 1–255 means failure. Scripts make decisions by checking `$?`.

first_principles.problem: A script carries on after a failed download and deploys an empty file, because nothing checked whether the step worked.
truths: Exit status is the universal success signal.
`$?` is overwritten by the next command.
Different codes can mean different failures.
derivation: Check `$?` **immediately**, or test the command directly with `if cmd; then`.
Return **meaningful codes** from your own scripts with `exit N`.

analogy.title: A report card
analogy.story: Each command hands back a grade. Zero means passed and anything else says what went wrong.
analogy.breaks: Some tools use non-zero codes for non-errors. For example, grep returns 1 when there's no match.

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: The deploy never runs on a missing artifact.

code.text:
if ! curl -fsS -o app.tar.gz "$URL"; then
  echo "download failed" >&2; exit 2
fi

conditional-execution-and.core: `a && b` runs b only if a succeeded; `a || b` runs b only if a failed. They give you one-line logic based on exit codes.

first_principles.problem: Writing a full if/then/fi for every 'do this, else complain' is verbose.
truths: Every command returns an exit code.
&& and || short-circuit.
Concise isn't always clearer.
derivation: `a && b || c` is **not** if/else: c also runs if b fails.

analogy.title: Domino rules
analogy.story: &&: knock over the next domino only if this one fell. ||: knock it over only if this one stayed standing.
analogy.breaks: Chaining both is a trap. Use a real if/else when the logic matters.

example.title: Build-then-deploy guard
example.scenario: Deploy only if the tests pass; otherwise alert.

steps.label: Caveat
steps.detail: notify also fires if the deploy itself fails, which may be what you want, but be deliberate about it.

code.text: make test && make deploy || notify "pipeline failed"

check.q: Is `a && b || c` the same as if a then b else c?
check.a: No. c also runs when b fails.

writing-robust-scripts-set-e-set-u-and-p.core: `set -euo pipefail` makes Bash fail fast: it exits on errors (-e), on unset variables (-u), and when any stage of a pipe fails (pipefail).

first_principles.problem: By default Bash runs every line even after failures. `rm -rf "$DIR/"` with an empty DIR becomes `rm -rf /`.
truths: Bash's defaults favour carrying on over being safe.
Unset variables expand silently to empty.
A pipeline's status is only its last command's.
derivation: `set -o pipefail`: **any pipe stage failing** fails the pipeline.
Put all three at the top of every script.

analogy.title: A circuit breaker
analogy.story: Instead of letting a short circuit burn the house down, the breaker trips the moment something goes wrong.
mapping: Deleted data or a bad deploy
analogy.breaks: `-e` has exceptions (inside if conditions and && chains), so it's a safety net, not a guarantee.

example.title: The empty-variable rm

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: The script stops with an error instead of wiping the root directory.

example.outcome: failures stop the script instead of cascading.

check.a: Without it, `false | true` succeeds because only the last command's status counts.

signal-trapping-cleaning-up-your-mess.core: `trap` registers cleanup code that runs when the script exits or is interrupted, so temp files and locks never get left behind.

first_principles.problem: Ctrl+C halfway through leaves gigabytes of temp files and a stale lock, because the cleanup at the end never ran.
truths: Scripts can be interrupted at any point.
Cleanup at the end of a script is skipped on early exit.
Signals can be caught.
derivation: `trap cleanup EXIT` runs it on **any exit**.
Also trap **INT and TERM** if you need specific behaviour.

analogy.title: A hotel's checkout process
analogy.story: However a guest leaves, early or late, housekeeping always resets the room.
analogy.breaks: SIGKILL (kill -9) can't be trapped, so nothing runs.

example.title: Temp workspace that always disappears
example.scenario: mktemp plus a trap on EXIT.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No orphaned files, however the script ends.

code.text:
TMP=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT
curl -o "$TMP/big.iso" "$URL"
# ... Ctrl+C here still cleans up

example.outcome: scripts leave the system as they found it.

check.q: Why trap EXIT rather than just putting cleanup at the end?
check.a: EXIT fires on every exit path, including errors and interrupts.

parameter-expansion-basics.core: `${var...}` expansions transform or validate a variable as you use it: defaults, required checks and lengths, with no external tools.

first_principles.problem: Scripts crash or misbehave when an optional variable is unset, and checking every one with if-blocks clutters the code.
truths: Variables are often optional.
Required inputs should fail loudly.
A built-in is faster than spawning a process.

analogy.title: A form with prefilled and required fields
analogy.story: Some fields come prefilled, and others won't submit until you fill them in.
analogy.breaks: Without the colon (e.g. `-`) an empty-but-set variable doesn't trigger the default.

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: ENV falls back to staging, and a missing token stops the script immediately with a clear message.

example.outcome: input handling in one line each.

check.a: Exits the script with msg if X is unset or empty.

advanced-parameter-expansion-string-mani.core: Bash can cut strings natively: `#`/`##` strip a prefix, `%`/`%%` strip a suffix, and `/` replaces text. That's faster than calling sed or awk.

first_principles.problem: Calling `basename`, `cut` or `sed` in a loop over thousands of files spawns thousands of processes.
truths: Each external command is a new process.
Most path and string edits are prefix or suffix cuts.
Built-ins are portable within Bash.

analogy.title: Trimming with scissors
analogy.story: Snip from the front (#) or the back (%). A double snip (## or %%) cuts as much as possible.
analogy.breaks: Patterns here are globs, not regexes.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No subprocesses, so it's instant even across 10k files.

check.q: How do you get a file's extension-less name?

arrays-working-with-lists.core: Indexed arrays hold lists safely. `"${arr[@]}"` expands to every element as a separate word, even when elements contain spaces.

first_principles.problem: Storing a list in a space-separated string breaks as soon as a filename contains a space.
truths: Word splitting breaks on whitespace.
Lists of things are common.
Quoting preserves boundaries.

analogy.title: Labelled egg carton slots
analogy.story: Each item sits in its own slot, so a large egg never spills into its neighbour.
analogy.breaks: Bash arrays are one-dimensional. For nested data, use another language.

example.title: Safe argument building
example.scenario: Optional flags collected into an array.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each argument stays intact, so there are no quoting bugs.

check.a: So each element expands to exactly one argument, even if it contains spaces.

associative-arrays-dictionaries-in-bash.core: Bash 4+ supports key→value maps through `declare -A`. Use them for lookups like 'environment → hostname' without long case statements.

first_principles.problem: Mapping names to values with if/elif chains or parallel arrays is clumsy and error-prone.
truths: Lookup by name is a common need.
Bash only treats a variable as a map if you declare it with -A.
macOS ships Bash 3 by default.

analogy.title: A phone book
analogy.story: Look up a name and get the number directly, with no scanning down a list.
analogy.breaks: Key order is not guaranteed, and macOS's default Bash 3 doesn't support associative arrays.

example.title: Environment → endpoint
example.scenario: Choose the API host by environment.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Adding an environment is one entry, not another branch.

check.q: What happens if you forget declare -A?
check.a: Bash treats it as an indexed array, so string keys evaluate to index 0 and overwrite each other.

debugging-the-x-ray-vision-set-x-and-bey.core: `set -x` prints every command after expansion and before it runs, so you see exactly what Bash executes. ShellCheck finds bugs before you run anything.

first_principles.problem: Scattering echo statements around is slow and still doesn't show how variables actually expanded.
truths: Bugs often come from how expansion behaves.
Seeing the expanded command reveals them.
Static analysis catches common mistakes.
derivation: Run `bash -x script` or **`set -x` / `set +x`** around the suspect region.

analogy.title: An X-ray
analogy.story: You see the bones (the actual commands), not just the skin (the source code).
analogy.breaks: set -x can print secrets into logs, so turn it off around sensitive commands.

example.title: Why does the glob not match?

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: The trace shows SRC was empty, so the command became cp /*.log.

example.outcome: you can see bugs instead of guessing at them.

check.q: What does set -x show that echo can't easily show?
check.a: Each command with its variables and globs already expanded, exactly as executed.
